summary.text: The strongest convergent signal in ulcerative colitis mucosa is the neutrophil chemokine axis built around CXCR2, its partner receptor CXCR1 and their ligand CXCL8. CXCR2 ranks first in the integrated ranking: it is up in the pooled meta-analysis of five cohorts [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264], higher in inflamed than non-inflamed mucosa of the same patient [gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.6972], carries Open Targets genetic support with an overall UC association of [gene=CXCR2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.5345], and has small-molecule antagonists that reached late clinical stages (reparixin, navarixin, ladarixin, SX-682), none of them in UC. CXCL8 shows an even larger mucosal increase [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.704] and is the best literature-supported node of the axis, but lacks genetic support. This is the only candidate in which expression, replication, inflammation, genetics, literature and druggability all agree.

The most reproducible losses are epithelial: genes of ketogenesis, ion transport and the tight junction fall in every cohort, led by CLDN8 [gene=CLDN8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-4.5181], HMGCS2 [gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.5845] and SLC26A2 [gene=SLC26A2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.4959]. These describe failure of the differentiated colonocyte and are best read as tissue biomarkers of injury rather than drug targets.

Known UC targets behave as positive controls with a different evidence profile. JAK2 has one of the strongest Open Targets UC associations [gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318] but only a small mucosal change [gene=JAK2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=0.872], and IL23R has strong genetic association [gene=IL23R; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.5997] while not appearing in the expression-driven ranking at all. Validated targets of signalling pathways therefore need not be transcriptionally prominent in biopsies, and the absence of a large fold change should not be used to discard a candidate.

The largest increases outside the chemokine axis are biomarker-type genes without genetic support: CHI3L1 [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.714], the calprotectin subunit S100A8 [gene=S100A8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.6467], DUOX2 [gene=DUOX2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.3213] and the matrix metalloproteinases. Most are neutrophil, macrophage or stress-response products, so they track inflammatory activity well but their bulk increase likely reflects infiltrating cells; IDO1 and OSMR sit between the two groups, with drugs in other indications and plausible mechanisms but weaker or absent genetics.

expression.text: A random-effects meta-analysis of five biopsy cohorts (one RNA-seq discovery cohort and four microarray cohorts) identifies a core set of genes that change in the same direction in every cohort. Among the up-regulated genes the largest pooled effects belong to CHI3L1 [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.714], S100A8 [gene=S100A8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.6467], DUOX2 [gene=DUOX2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.3213] and CXCL8 [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.704], together with IDO1 [gene=IDO1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.445] and several matrix metalloproteinases. Functionally these genes describe antimicrobial and oxidative defence (DUOX2, calprotectin), neutrophil recruitment (CXCL8 and its receptors CXCR1 and CXCR2), interferon-driven tryptophan catabolism (IDO1) and tissue remodelling (MMP family).

The down-regulated side is dominated by differentiated epithelial functions. The tight-junction protein CLDN8 shows the largest pooled decrease [gene=CLDN8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-4.5181], followed by the ketogenic enzyme HMGCS2 [gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.5845] and the sulphate transporter SLC26A2 [gene=SLC26A2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.4959]. Loss of HMGCS2, which makes ketone bodies from butyrate-derived acetyl-CoA, points to failure of the colonocyte energy metabolism, and loss of CLDN8 and SLC26A2 to a weakened barrier and ion transport. These genes are consistent markers of epithelial injury, not candidate drug targets.

Druggable receptors change less than these marker genes. CXCR2 [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264], OSMR [gene=OSMR; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.042], FCGR2A [gene=FCGR2A; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=1.5938] and CCL2 [gene=CCL2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.28] are all up, but CCL2 is measured in only four cohorts, and JAK2 is significant in all five cohorts with only a small effect [gene=JAK2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=0.872]. Pooled estimates are mostly highly heterogeneous across cohorts: direction is consistent but effect size differs, partly because microarray fold changes are compressed relative to RNA-seq.

inflammation.text: Comparing inflamed with non-inflamed mucosa of the same patients in the MSCCR discovery cohort shows that most top genes are driven by local inflammation. The neutrophil axis rises sharply within patients, for CXCR1 [gene=CXCR1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.1931], CXCL8 [gene=CXCL8; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.9681] and S100A8 [gene=S100A8; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.8038], as do CHI3L1 [gene=CHI3L1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.6182], MMP7 [gene=MMP7; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.8797] and IDO1 [gene=IDO1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.6828]. On the epithelial side HMGCS2 falls within patients [gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=-1.9508] while non-inflamed mucosa does not differ from control (padj [gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; padj=0.675]), so its loss is a consequence of active inflammation rather than a constitutive defect. CCL2 has only a small paired change [gene=CCL2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=0.7378].

A minority of changes are already present in non-inflamed mucosa. DUOX2 is modestly raised in non-inflamed mucosa versus control [gene=DUOX2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.8129] and increases further with inflammation [gene=DUOX2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.4812], suggesting an epithelial stress state that precedes overt inflammation, whereas CXCR2 shows only a small rise outside inflamed tissue [gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.6399]. Because bulk biopsy RNA mixes cell types, increases of immune genes such as CXCR1, CXCR2, CXCL8, S100A8 and IDO1 may come from infiltrating neutrophils and myeloid cells rather than from regulation within resident cells; cell composition is analysed later.

replication.text: Changes found in the MSCCR RNA-seq discovery cohort reproduce well in the four microarray cohorts (UNIFI, PURSUIT-SC and two Leuven cohorts): every gene in the top of the convergence ranking except CCL2 changes in the same direction in all five cohorts. Replication is clearest where heterogeneity is low: SERPINB5 rises in the discovery cohort [gene=SERPINB5; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_control; log2fc=3.0898] and by a similar amount in the Leuven infliximab cohort [gene=SERPINB5; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE16879; layer=rna; cohort=GSE16879; contrast=uc_vs_control; log2fc=3.229], giving a pooled heterogeneity of only [gene=SERPINB5; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; i2=0.119] and a pooled padj of [gene=SERPINB5; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; padj=4.81e-135]. For most other genes direction replicates but magnitude does not: CLDN8 falls in the discovery cohort [gene=CLDN8; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_control; log2fc=-4.4028] and even more in UNIFI [gene=CLDN8; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE206285; layer=rna; cohort=GSE206285; contrast=uc_vs_control; log2fc=-5.9822], so cross-cohort comparisons should rely on direction and significance rather than on effect size.

literature.text: Literature support from the curated abstract corpus is concentrated on expression-led genes and is almost entirely bioinformatic or preclinical. CXCL8 is the best-supported node of the chemokine axis, with PMID:33706134 placing the CXCL8 axis with its receptors CXCR1 and CXCR2 in UC pathogenesis through PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signalling. IDO1 has the most direct mechanistic study (PMID:40370742): it is elevated in UC, drives M1 macrophage polarisation through the GRP78-XBP1 endoplasmic-reticulum stress pathway, and a methyl-tryptophan IDO inhibitor ameliorated DSS colitis in mice. CHI3L1 is reported to promote macrophage pyroptosis through BCAT1 and NF-kappaB (PMID:41314595), and AQP9, which is predominantly neutrophil-expressed, is reported to promote neutrophil extracellular trap formation through JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis in mouse colitis (PMID:41504039), so its tissue signal reflects neutrophil infiltration.

For biomarkers, MMP1 tracks treatment response: transcripts modified by mirikizumab and correlated with the modified Mayo, Geboes and Robarts indices include MMP1, MMP3, S100A8 and IL1B (PMID:36881820), and MMP1 is a bioinformatic hub gene associated with macrophage infiltration together with CD274, NCF2 and PLAU (PMID:41368353). S100A9 is reported to perform well for diagnosing active UC (PMID:38448514), SLC26A2 is down in active UC and correlates with Mayo score and PUCAI (PMID:40002875), and DUOX2 is among the most elevated proteins in inflamed biopsies (PMID:39280905). A notable negative result is that the top-ranked receptors have essentially no literature: CXCR2 appears only as a hub gene in active UC (PMID:38448514), and neither CXCR1 nor CXCR2 antagonists have UC clinical evidence in the corpus; CD274, OSMR and JAK2 likewise have no extracted UC relations.

external.text: Among candidates with an approved UC drug, Open Targets genetics singles out JAK2 [gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318] and IL23R [gene=IL23R; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.5997], both established UC targets that act as positive controls for the genetic stream; neither is prominent in the biopsy transcriptome. Among expression-led candidates, CXCR2 combines genetic support with 'SM: Advanced Clinical' tractability and dual CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists (reparixin late-stage, navarixin, ladarixin, SX-682 earlier), CXCR1 shares those inhibitors with intermediate genetic support, and STRING links CXCR2 to CXCL8, CXCL1 and CXCL5 at very high confidence. FCGR2A has the strongest genetic association of the top ranking [gene=FCGR2A; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.87] and CCL2 also has genetic support [gene=CCL2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.5829], but neither has a drug in a UC-relevant setting.

Expression-led candidates without genetic support fall into two groups. Some have drugs in other indications: anti-IL-8 antibodies for CXCL8, epacadostat and linrodostat for IDO1, vixarelimab for OSMR (antibody tractability 'AB: Advanced Clinical'), broad MMP inhibitors such as marimastat for the MMP family, and PD-L1 antibodies for CD274, where checkpoint blockade would act in the wrong direction for colitis. Others have no drug at all: CHI3L1, CXCL1, CXCL5 and the calprotectin subunits S100A8 and S100A9 are among the most reproducible increases but have neither genetic association nor a returned compound, which fits a biomarker rather than a target role.

integration.text: The streams agree most strongly on the neutrophil chemokine axis. CXCR2 is the only candidate supported by all six streams; CXCL8 adds the largest mucosal increase of the axis and the best literature, CXCR1 adds the largest within-patient rise, and STRING ties CXCL1 and CXCL5 to the same receptor. Expression and literature also agree on the epithelial injury signature (HMGCS2, CLDN8, SLC26A2) and on myeloid biomarkers (CHI3L1, S100A8, S100A9, MMP1), where published work and the transcriptome point the same way but genetics is silent.

The main disagreement is between genetics and expression. The genetically strongest UC targets, JAK2 and IL23R, are transcriptionally modest or absent from the ranking, while the largest expression changes (CHI3L1, DUOX2, S100A8, MMPs, CXCL8) have no genetic association. Literature and genetics also diverge: CXCR2, CXCR1, CD274 and OSMR have genetic or tractability support but almost no UC literature, whereas the best-studied genes in the corpus (IDO1, CHI3L1, AQP9) are expression-led with no genetics. The convergence score rewards genes that bridge these streams, which is why receptors with modest fold changes (CXCR2, CD274, FCGR2A) rank above genes with larger but genetically unsupported changes.

targets.rationale: Ranked first and the only gene supported by all six streams: reproducibly up [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264], higher in inflamed mucosa, Open Targets genetic support and clinical-stage small-molecule antagonists in other indications. Literature is almost absent and the bulk rise likely reflects neutrophil infiltration, so efficacy in UC is untested.

Ligand of CXCR1 and CXCR2 with a large reproducible increase [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.704], a strong within-patient rise and the best literature support of the axis; anti-IL-8 antibodies reached clinical stage. Placed second despite lacking genetic support because it is the mechanistic hub of the top candidate.

Second receptor of the axis, sharing the dual CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists, with intermediate genetic support and the largest within-patient rise of the receptors [gene=CXCR1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.1931]. Its pooled effect is smaller and more heterogeneous than CXCR2, hence third.

Positive control: JAK inhibition is an established UC therapy. Strong Open Targets association [gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318] with only a small mucosal change; ranked high on genetics and clinical precedent rather than on expression, which the numeric ranking underweights.

Positive control: the IL23R pathway is targeted by approved UC biologics. Strong genetic association [gene=IL23R; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.5997] but absent from the expression-driven ranking; included to show that genetics-led targets are not captured by biopsy transcriptomics.

Oncostatin M receptor is up [gene=OSMR; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.042] with genetic association, antibody tractability and a clinical-stage antibody (vixarelimab); a mirikizumab study lists it among transcripts of resistance to current therapies. Within-patient change is modest and its cellular source must be checked.

Strongly induced interferon-response gene [gene=IDO1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.445] with the most direct mechanistic literature (macrophage polarisation, inhibitor efficacy in mouse colitis) and oncology inhibitors; no genetic support and single-group evidence, so placed below the genetically supported targets.

Calprotectin subunit with one of the largest reproducible increases [gene=S100A8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.6467] and a clear within-patient rise; tissue-level support for faecal calprotectin, a positive control among biomarkers. Neutrophil-derived, so it measures infiltration.

Largest pooled increase among top genes [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.714], strongly inflammation-linked within patients and supported by preclinical pyroptosis literature, but with no genetics and no drug; best used as a tissue activity marker.

Epithelial ketogenesis enzyme lost in all cohorts [gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.5845] and further within inflamed mucosa, but normal in non-inflamed mucosa: a marker of active epithelial metabolic failure rather than a target.
Tight-junction gene with the largest pooled decrease [gene=CLDN8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-4.5181], down in every cohort; a barrier-injury biomarker.

Large reproducible increase [gene=DUOX2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.3213] and one of few genes already raised in non-inflamed mucosa, making it a candidate marker of pre-inflammatory epithelial stress; proteomic and diagnostic literature agree, but there is no specific drug.

Representative of the replicated MMP family; tracks clinical and histological response to mirikizumab in published work and has no genetic support. Broad MMP inhibitors exist but are not UC-specific, so it is listed as a response biomarker.

Exploratory: strongest genetic association in the top of the ranking [gene=FCGR2A; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.87] with a modest, replicated expression increase, but no UC-relevant drug and no literature in the corpus; ranked last for lack of mechanistic and pharmacological support.

limitations.text: Bulk biopsy transcriptomes mix cell types; increases of neutrophil and myeloid genes (CXCR1, CXCR2, CXCL8, S100A8, S100A9, AQP9, CHI3L1) may reflect cell infiltration rather than regulation within resident cells. Cell-composition analysis is pending.
Pooled estimates are highly heterogeneous for most genes, and microarray fold changes are compressed relative to RNA-seq; direction and significance are more reliable than effect size across cohorts.
Paired inflamed versus non-inflamed contrasts and the non-inflamed versus control contrast come from a single cohort (MSCCR).

Literature relations were extracted from a small abstract corpus (about three hundred abstracts); relation counts do not measure clinical importance, most biomarker claims come from bioinformatic signatures with limited validation, and diagnostic performance values were not quantified. The PubMed connector was unavailable, so no additional literature checks were made.
Drug stages are the Open Targets maximum clinical stage in any indication, not UC trials. IL23R and TNF are outside the convergence ranking, so their expression was not quantified here.

Several genes with strong expression changes (SLC6A14, DEFB4A, SAA2, TMIGD1) are measured in only two to four cohorts and were not prioritised. Expression and genetic association do not establish causality, efficacy or target safety.
